Article Title: ‘Stranded Umrah pilgrims being assisted’: Rijiju shares helpline numbers for Indians in Saudi Arabia
Article Text:
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju on Friday said that the stranded Umrah pilgrims have returned to India safely

NEW DELHI: Union minister for parliamentary affairs Kiren Rijiju on Friday said Indian authorities were helping Umrah pilgrims stranded in Saudi Arabia return home, adding that those affected had reached India safely while arrangements were underway for others awaiting assistance.In a post on X, Rijiju said more than 10,000 other Umrah pilgrims had also returned to India earlier. He shared contact details of round-the-clock control rooms at the Indian Embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate General in Jeddah for nationals requiring help.“The government is always proactive on the issues and concerns of Indian citizens. The stranded Umrah pilgrims have returned to India safely, in addition to more than 10,000 normal Umrah pilgrims who have returned earlier. Remaining Umrah pilgrims are being assisted,” Rijiju wrote.The Embassy of India in Riyadh can be contacted at +966-554412016 and +966-542126784. Its toll-free number, 8002471234, is available for calls from within Saudi Arabia. WhatsApp messages can be sent to +966-536216082.The Consulate General of India in Jeddah can be reached at +966-12-2614093 and +966-556122301. Its WhatsApp number for messages is +966-536209704.Earlier, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said around 3,000 stranded Indian Umrah pilgrims had travelled back from Saudi Arabia over the preceding week, with Indian diplomatic missions coordinating with airlines and tour operators to facilitate their return.India is coordinating with airlines and tour operators to facilitate the early return of Indian pilgrims stranded in Saudi Arabia amid the regional security situation,
Article Summary: Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju on Friday said Indian authorities were helping Umrah pilgrims stranded in Saudi Arabia return home. He said those affected had reached India safely while arrangements were underway for others awaiting assistance. He shared contact details of round-the-clock control rooms at the Indian Embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate General in Jeddah.

Article Title: 'Can't drive into future looking at rearview mirror': India calls for urgent UNSC reforms
Article Text:
India's Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Parvathaneni Harish

India has called for urgent reforms to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), warning that its 80-year-old structure is struggling to address some of the world’s gravest conflicts. New Delhi said the Council’s composition must reflect present-day global realities, arguing that its post-Second World War framework no longer adequately represents the international community.According to news agency PTI, India’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, said on Thursday that the authority inherited from the Second World War could no longer compensate for the Council’s lack of representative membership.“The cost is already visible. Eighty years on, the Organisation is struggling to deliver peace and reconciliation in some of the gravest conflicts before the Council,” Parvathaneni said while addressing the UN General Assembly on equitable representation and an expansion of the Security Council.He added that “the authority derived from a victory eight decades ago cannot compensate for the deficit in legitimacy of an unrepresentative Security Council today.”The Indian envoy argued that 1945, when the UN was established after the Second World War, could not remain the sole reference point for global governance.“No war, especially one that took place over 80 years ago, should determine today’s state of the world,” he said.“History can be a guide for what not to do. It cannot determine today’s choices for what needs to be done to face contemporary challenges. We cannot reasonably drive into the future by constantly looking at the rearview mirror,” he added.Parvathaneni also highlighted India’s contribution to the World Wars, arguing that the sacrifices of several nations had not received adequate recognition in the post-war international order.“An organisation crafted of the victors, for the victors and by the victors did not, obviously, care to include the concerns of the victims,” he said, calling for the Security Council to evolve “for the sake of its own relevance”.According to PTI, he noted that around 2.5 million Indians participated in the Second World War, with approximately 90,000 dying in military service. He also referred to the Bengal famine, which he attributed to colonial wartime policies.India further pointed to the under-representation of Asia-Pacific, Africa and Latin America. The Asia-Pacific region accounts for more than 60 per cent of the world’s population but has only one permanent seat on the Council, alongside a fluctuating elected representation.“Reform is not the settlement of old scores. It is an investment in a Council that all Member States can trust, and which would be stronger as a result,” Parvathaneni said.The 15-member UNSC comprises five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — with veto powers, alongside 10 elected members serving two-year terms.India supports expanding both permanent and non-permanent membership, arguing that changes limited to elected seats would leave the central imbalance intact.Criticising the pace of negotiations, Parvathaneni said, “That is not negotiation; it is merely perpetuation of status quo.”He added, “Convergences are not consensus, and the search for a lowest common denominator must not become an excuse for cosmetically tinkering with the existing structure while calling it reform.”India also maintained that any permanent membership expansion must address the veto question fairly. “A two-tier permanent membership would only institutionalise inequality,” he said.
Article Summary: India has called for urgent reforms to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) New Delhi said the Council’s composition must reflect present-day global realities. The 15-member UNSC comprises five permanent members with veto powers, alongside 10 elected members serving two-year terms.

Article Title: 'Shaurya commandos' prepared: ITBP chief flags ‘ongoing’ China faceoff along Arunachal border
Article Text:
Addressing at an ITBP base in Alwar, Rajasthan, ahead of the force’s 65th Raising Day on October 24.

Congress targets Centre

The Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) has raised a new combat unit, the Shaurya commandos, who have demonstrated their capabilities during the “ongoing” faceoff with Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) troops at multiple locations in Arunachal Pradesh, ITBP chief Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor said on Thursday.Kapoor said the commandos would be deployed in every border battalion as the force strengthens its combat readiness along the 3,488-km Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China. The ITBP chief’s remarks came as the force steps up its modernisation drive, with a greater focus on emerging warfare technologies and specialised training.Addressing personnel at an ITBP base in Alwar, Rajasthan, ahead of the force’s 65th Raising Day on October 24, Kapoor said traditional methods of warfare were no longer sufficient to counter China, which he described as India’s “biggest adversary”.The force has raised drone platoons in all its border-guarding battalions and is training personnel to operate drones and develop the technology. Kapoor said the ITBP had received Rs 400 crore in government funding, with 70% earmarked for strengthening its drone warfare capabilities. The Ministry of Home Affairs has also given in-principle approval to a Rs 4,000-crore modernisation plan, including Rs 1,000 crore for drone and anti-drone systems.The ITBP has also developed a new ‘Strike’ course to prepare personnel for combat situations similar to the June 2020 Galwan Valley clash. Kapoor said the entire force would undergo the training by the end of 2027.During the Galwan clash in eastern Ladakh, 20 Indian soldiers were killed in a violent confrontation with Chinese troops. China later acknowledged the deaths of four of its soldiers.Beyond combat training and technology, the force is also strengthening infrastructure at forward locations. Kapoor said the ITBP was building underground shelters in border areas to reduce vulnerabilities in the event of a conflict, as above-ground structures could become targets during a war.The force is also upgrading troop facilities in high-altitude areas, including insulating barracks, installing solar water heaters and providing generator sets to ensure electricity at remote posts. It has introduced cold-start kits to help vehicles start in freezing conditions.Kapoor said these measures were part of a broader plan to develop the ITBP into a specialised high-altitude mountain-fighting force capable of responding to evolving security challenges along the China border.Congress MP Jairam Ramesh accused the Centre of making concessions to China and failing to address concerns over border tensions in Arunachal Pradesh. He also alleged that India had lost access to certain patrolling points in the region.In a post on X, Ramesh cited the Director General of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) praising the force’s performance during recent face-offs with China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) in Arunachal Pradesh. He questioned the government’s silence on the reported incidents, alleging that neither the Prime Minister nor his establishment had publicly addressed the matter.The Congress leader also flagged China’s moves to rename places in Arunachal Pradesh and its reported construction of a 60,000-MW dam, "Local residents have reported that, just like in Ladakh, several patrolling points have once again slipped from our control. China is relentlessly renaming our towns in Arunachal Pradesh and constructing a 60,000 MW dam, which poses a major threat to our ecology and water security. "
Article Summary: ITBP chief Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor says Shaurya commandos will be deployed in every border battalion. He says traditional methods of warfare are no longer sufficient to counter China. The ITBP has received Rs 400 crore in government funding, with 70% earmarked for strengthening its drone warfare capabilities. The Ministry of Home Affairs has also given in-principle approval to a Rs 4,000-crore modernisation plan.

Article Title: Dark homes, dry taps, idle factories: Gurgaon hit by 16-hour power cuts amid strike
Article Text:
Thousands of households in Gurgaon faced power and water outages due to a strike by electricity department employees.

DHBVN employees during the strike on Thursday

Industrialists said repeated calls to DHBVN officials had failed to resolve the disruption, leaving workers and machinery idle

No electricity, no water

- General picture of Industrial workers.______________Picture by TOI

Nearly 1,800 manufacturing units hit; industrialists fear losses worth crores

Old Gurgaon worst hit as feeders remain out of service

Helplines fail to provide relief as officials struggle to respond

Why are electricity employees on strike?

Govt says strike unnecessary, promises legal battle against licence

Power engineers seek cabinet decision to rule out parallel licences





GURGAON: Thousands of households went without electricity and water, nearly 1,800 manufacturing units faced disruption, and residents took to the streets as a three-day strike by Haryana's electricity department employees crippled power supply across Gurgaon on Thursday.With breakdown complaints going unattended, inverters running out of charge and industrial units struggling to keep production lines operational, the disruption exposed the city's dependence on an uninterrupted electricity supply for even its most basic needs.The strike, called to protest the Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission's (HERC) decision to grant a parallel electricity distribution licence to private company Eleven Power for Gurgaon and Nuh, began affecting supplies from Wednesday night.By Thursday, power cuts had spread across residential colonies, industrial clusters and rural areas, with residents complaining that repeated calls to electricity officials and helplines had failed to bring relief.In several localities, prolonged outages also hit water supply as electricity-dependent boosting stations and household motors stopped functioning. While some residents managed with water stored in tanks, others said their reserves would last only a few hours.In industrial areas, manufacturers turned to diesel generator sets, but these offered only temporary relief, with prolonged use restricted by overheating, cooling requirements and air pollution control norms.The scale of the disruption was reflected in the complaints received by Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam (DHBVN). An official said the department received more than 3,000 complaints within the first 12 hours of the strike, while DHBVN's helplines received around 5,000 outage complaints on Thursday.Residents, however, alleged that neither the helplines nor the officials responsible for local supply were responding adequately.Gurgaon, which has around 8.5 lakh electricity consumers, saw widespread disruption, particularly in Old Gurgaon. Residents said more than 50,000 households in the area were affected on Thursday, with several localities continuing to face outages even after hours of waiting. The agitation also affected Faridabad and Nuh, where residential areas and industrial units reported power cuts.For thousands of families, the immediate concern was no longer just the absence of electricity but the inability to carry out everyday activities, from cooking and studying to securing drinking water.In Sector 9A, around 6,000 families were affected after power supply snapped around 3.30am on Thursday. The outage also affected the boosting station supplying the area, leaving households without water. More than 16 hours later, supply had still not been restored, according to Suraj Bhola, general secretary of the Sector 9A residents' welfare association (RWA).“I have called the officials nearly 50 times, but nobody is responding. There is no electricity at our homes. Inverters have run out, and now there is no water either because the boosting station is affected. How are people supposed to manage their daily needs?” Bhola said.He alleged that the junior engineer was not answering calls, while the sub-divisional officer had cited the strike. The helpline number provided by the district administration had also failed to secure relief, he said. With no clarity on when electricity would return, residents were unable to plan their day or arrange alternative water supplies. Tankers, he added, were also difficult to find.In Hari Nagar, more than 7,000 families were affected after power supply went off around 10pm on Wednesday and remained disrupted for more than 16 hours, residents said. The accompanying water shortage left families struggling to meet basic needs.“People are suffering in their homes, children are struggling to study, and nobody is listening to us. Junior engineer (JE) and SDO are not answering calls. The office has been locked, and there is nobody available to address the complaints,” said Sumit Gujjar, Hari Nagar RWA president.While acknowledging employees' right to protest, Gujjar questioned the impact of the agitation on ordinary residents.“If employees have an issue with the govt, they should take it up with the govt instead of leaving residents without electricity and water,” he said.The uncertainty over restoration was equally distressing for residents of housing societies, where backup systems could not meet every household's needs.At Zara Aavaas, an affordable housing society, residents said power had been unavailable since 5.30am. The backup system covered essential services such as lifts but did not provide electricity to individual flats.Hemant Sharma, a resident, said the outage had created additional difficulties as pollution levels rose and restrictions under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) came into force.“On one hand, pollution levels are increasing and GRAP restrictions are in place, while on the other, the prolonged power outage has forced people to run diesel gensets. Many residents have to work from home, but how are they supposed to work without electricity for so many hours? It is even more difficult for people with medical conditions who may depend on electrical equipment or need a comfortable indoor environment,” he said.Residents of Lotus Homz also struggled as the outage continued through the day.“There has been no power supply since 5am. It has become difficult to manage even basic household chores. Even inverter ran out of battery and I had to cook dinner using the light from my mobile phone. We don’t even know when the electricity will be restored. The management has asked residents to move to the community hall, but while we somehow managed today, we don’t know what will happen tomorrow if the power supply remains disrupted,” said resident Anu Gulati.In Rajendra Park, Bhimgarh Kheri and areas near Gurgaon railway station, residents who had been without electricity since 10am staged a protest near the railway station road bridge on Thursday evening. By around 8pm, with the outage stretching to nearly 10 hours, a large number of men and women had taken to the road and raised slogans against the power department.Police personnel reached the spot to pacify the protesters, but residents refused to disperse until electricity was restored. They said the outage had disrupted household work and water supply.“There is no electricity, and there is no water in our homes. How are we supposed to run the water motor without power?” said Rupa, a resident.Residents in Faridabad's New Industrial Township-2 area also took to the streets demanding restoration of power. Police intervened after receiving information about a road blockade and dispersed the protesters after pacifying them. In Nuh, the disruption affected several areas, including Punhana, Nagina and Firozpur Jhirka.The power crisis extended beyond homes, threatening production schedules and deliveries across Gurgaon's industrial belt.Nearly 1,800 manufacturing units in the Sector 37 and Kadipur industrial areas faced disruption after power cuts began around 10pm on Wednesday. Industrial units in Basai were also affected, with manufacturers reporting that machinery had stopped and production lines had come to a halt.The affected businesses include textile units, export houses, auto component manufacturers and suppliers of food to corporate and commercial establishments. Industrialists warned that a prolonged disruption could lead to losses running into crores of rupees, while delays in production could affect the availability of finished goods and timely delivery of supplies.Deepak Maini, chairman of the Progressive Federation of Trade and Industry (PFTI), said there had been no power supply in Sector 37 since 10pm on Wednesday.“Power cuts at industrial units have brought machinery and production to a halt, impacting business operations. With operations suspended across hundreds of units, the risk of losses has increased,” Maini said.Manufacturers attempted to switch to diesel generator sets, but said these could not sustain continuous industrial operations. Generators need cooling breaks after running for several hours, interrupting production and making them unsuitable as a long-term replacement for grid electricity.“A generator is meant for backup, not regular power supply. After running for several hours, it heats up and needs to be switched off to cool down,” industrialist Vikrant Gupta said.The situation was further complicated by the enforcement of GRAP from Wednesday. With restrictions on generator sets intended to control air pollution in the National Capital Region, industrialists said they faced a difficult choice between keeping operations running and complying with pollution-control requirements. Non-compliant generator sets could face action under the applicable norms.“How are we supposed to run our operations amid so many disruptions? Power is basic to running an industry,” another industrialist said.Manufacturers said the crisis had also exposed the difficulties in getting faults repaired when the regular electricity workforce was unavailable. Maini said DHBVN officials had expressed their inability to resolve the problems, while private vendors could not be engaged to work on high-tension lines and feeders.He argued that the immediate priority should be uninterrupted electricity, regardless of the provider.“If DHBVN is unable to provide the service, there is nothing wrong with allowing private players. We want an uninterrupted power supply, whoever provides it — the govt or a private player,” Maini said.He added that frequent outages had already become a persistent problem for manufacturers, requiring repeated maintenance interventions and disrupting production schedules.Industrialist PK Gupta said the responsibility for ensuring electricity supply rested with the government.“It is the govt’s responsibility to ensure power supply. We pay taxes to the govt,” he said.Industrialists urged the state government to consider invoking the Essential Services Maintenance Act (ESMA), if legally warranted, and make alternative arrangements to restore electricity. Their concerns highlighted the immediate economic cost of the strike even as the broader dispute centred on whether a private company should be allowed to distribute electricity alongside the state-owned discom.The disruption was more widespread in DHBVN's Circle 1, which covers Old Gurgaon, sectors 9 and 10, and Kadipur, than in Circle 2, which includes parts of South City, Sohna and sectors along Golf Course Road.In Circle 1, 12 of the 530 11kV feeders were out of service on Thursday. In Circle 2, 14 of the 750 feeders were shut down.Power supply remained disrupted in nearly 50 localities, including Palam Vihar, New Palam Vihar, Sai Kunj, Chandan Vihar, Ashok Vihar, sectors 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 7 Extension, Hari Nagar, Gandhi Nagar, Rajendra Park, Vishnu Garden, Surat Nagar, Dhanwapur, Sushant Lok 2 and 3, Manesar, Sohna and Taoru.Sector 9A remained among the worst-affected areas, with residents reporting that power had not returned even after several hours. In Sushant Lok 2, around 500 families in B block were without electricity from about 6am. Supply was restored in Sushant Lok around 2.30pm, but Sector 9A was still without power at the time of filing this report.The situation also deteriorated around Sohna and Nimauth power houses. Four feeders were out of service by 8am on Thursday, and the number rose to 12 by 3pm, affecting around 30 villages. Two urban feeders were also disrupted, affecting City-4, Gehlot Bihar and the MVN and Aekam residential societies.Officials said five of the 15 feeders serving rural areas and seven of the 39 urban feeders had been shut down by 3pm.The relatively better situation in parts of Circle 2 was attributed to an arrangement under which line maintenance in selected localities had been outsourced to a private company. Its workers continued attending to faults and breakdowns despite the strike.The arrangement covers areas such as Badshapur, Tikli, Bhondsi, Rithoj, parts of South City and sectors 14, 17, 18 and 23. However, it does not extend across the entire city. Substations and power houses continue to depend on DHBVN employees, limiting the extent to which outsourced maintenance can compensate for the absence of the regular workforce.DHBVN deployed around 100 workers hired through a contractor to repair faults, but the arrangement brought little relief, with workers reportedly struggling to identify the faults.Chief engineer PK Chauhan said the overwhelming participation of employees had made it difficult to handle complaints.“About 98% of DHBVN’s officers and employees are on strike. Even executive engineers and superintending engineers have joined it. The absence of staff is making it difficult to address electricity complaints. Senior officials have been informed about the situation,” he said.In Circle 1, 816 of 826 employees joined the strike, while 540 of 557 employees in Circle 2 stayed away from work. Outsourced staff and workers recruited through Haryana Kaushal Rozgar Nigam also joined the agitation. Superintending engineers Shyambir Saini and Manoj Yadav supported the protest.Subhash Kumar, SDO of Sohna DHBVN, said updates on outages were being shared with senior officials every hour.As complaints mounted, the district administration and electricity department faced criticism from residents who said they had no reliable way to find out when supply would be restored.On Wednesday evening, deputy commissioner Uttam Singh issued a press release listing contact numbers for consumers affected by outages. Residents said, however, that complaints made through toll-free numbers 1912 and 180010804334, as well as WhatsApp numbers 8813999708 and 9540954768, did not result in timely relief.The problem was compounded by the absence of employees at complaint centres, substations and offices at the sub-divisional, divisional and circle levels. The striking employees' joint front said many of these facilities had been largely deserted, while faults affecting 33kV and 11kV feeders remained unattended.The state government said arrangements were being made to maintain supply during the strike, with deputy commissioner Uttam Singh directing officials to prioritise essential services, including hospitals, water supply systems and the metro.But residents said the lack of clear information about restoration was making the disruption harder to manage. In areas where electricity had been unavailable for much of the day, exhausted inverter batteries and depleted water storage left families with few alternatives.The immediate trigger for the strike was HERC's October 19 order granting Eleven Power Private Limited a parallel electricity distribution licence for Gurgaon and Nuh for 25 years under Section 14 of the Electricity Act, 2003.The licence allows the company to distribute electricity in the two revenue districts alongside the existing state-owned distribution companies. The Haryana Bijli Karamchari and Engineers Joint Sangharsh Morcha called a three-day strike against the decision, arguing that the entry of a private distributor threatened the existing public distribution system.Around 40,000 electricity department employees across Haryana joined the strike, according to the unions, which said the agitation was not about salaries or allowances but about protecting public electricity infrastructure, employees' jobs and consumers' interests.Devender Singh Hooda, a senior leader of the joint front, said the movement was aimed at preventing the privatisation of electricity distribution and safeguarding farmers and ordinary consumers.The unions argued that a parallel distribution licence could weaken the revenue base of public utilities in an agriculture-dominated state. They warned that this could affect the ability of public discoms to provide affordable and reliable electricity, particularly to farmers and economically weaker sections in rural and urban areas.The unions also questioned the transparency of the regulatory process. They sought details of Eleven Power's experience, technical capabilities, capital investment, financial strength and eligibility, as well as public disclosure of the criteria used to assess its application. They demanded an impartial inquiry into the roles of the regulator and the company.Amarjeet Jakhar and Mukesh Bhayana said the agitation would continue until the decision was withdrawn. Jakhar said employees would decide whether to extend the strike beyond October 24 if their demands were not accepted.The movement also received support from several workers' and farmers' organisations. Most constituent organisations of the Samyukt Kisan Morcha, along with Sarv Karamchari Sangh Haryana and trade unions, including CITU, AITUC and INTUC, extended support and organised demonstrations at various locations.Subhash Lamba, vice-president of the Electricity Employees Federation of India (EEFI), and Shailendra Dubey, chairman of the All India Power Engineers Federation (AIPEF), also opposed the parallel licence.Lamba alleged that the Haryana government was attempting to undermine the agitation by bringing technical employees and supervisors from neighbouring states, including Punjab and Himachal Pradesh.“If the chief minister and the energy minister oppose privatisation and stand with electricity employees, why is a parallel distribution licence being granted to a private company in the first place?” he asked.He said the government needed to demonstrate its opposition through concrete action rather than assurances.The Haryana government has opposed the licensing decision and said it would challenge HERC's order before the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), seeking an immediate stay on its implementation.Chief minister Nayab Singh Saini said on Wednesday that the government would represent the employees' case before the tribunal. He also assured unions that lawyers trusted by the employees could be engaged to pursue the challenge.Saini held a review meeting with administrative secretaries and district officials through video conferencing to assess preparations for the three-day strike. He appealed to the unions to call off the agitation, saying the government's doors for dialogue remained open.Energy minister Anil Vij, meanwhile, termed the strike unnecessary, arguing that the licensing decision had been taken by the independent regulator rather than the state government.Vij said the government had opposed the move before HERC and would now challenge it before APTEL. He also said he was against privatisation because substantial public money had been invested in the existing electricity infrastructure and employees' jobs were at stake.“I am against privatisation because substantial public money has been invested in the infrastructure and employees’ jobs are at stake,” he said.Vij urged employees to return to work and participate in the legal challenge instead of continuing the strike. He offered to involve union representatives in preparing the government's case, including by allowing them to advise its lawyer, appoint their own counsel or recommend another lawyer.The government has maintained that it did not invite applications for privatising electricity distribution. However, Vij said the central law allows any eligible individual or company to apply for a distribution licence, and the decision to grant one rests with the regulator.The distinction has become central to the dispute: while the state government says it is opposed to the licence and intends to challenge it, the employees want the decision withdrawn and a clear policy ruling out parallel distribution licences anywhere in Haryana.The dispute escalated on Thursday as electricity engineers and employee representatives called on the state government to go beyond its proposed legal challenge and take a policy decision against parallel distribution licences.AIPEF chairman Shailendra Dubey, along with Haryana Power Engineers Association leaders Puneet Kundu and Ravinder Singh Ghanghas, urged chief minister Nayab Singh Saini to convene a cabinet meeting and announce a policy ruling out such licences anywhere in the state.Dubey said the government should use its statutory powers under the Electricity Act, 2003, to revoke the licence.The employee leaders questioned HERC's decision and alleged that it appeared to promote privatisation despite the state's stated opposition. They demanded transparency on the private company's qualifications and an impartial inquiry into the circumstances in which the licence was granted.The unions said their concerns extended beyond the immediate impact on jobs. They argued that allowing parallel distribution could undermine the financial position of state-owned utilities and eventually affect electricity affordability and reliability for ordinary consumers.The government, however, has maintained that it must challenge the regulator's decision through the appropriate legal process. Vij urged employees to end the strike and join that effort, while Saini assured them that the state would pursue the matter before APTEL.The impasse has left residents and businesses bearing the immediate cost of a dispute over the future structure of electricity distribution.For households, the consequences have been exhausted inverters, dry taps, disrupted routines and uncertainty over when power would return. For manufacturers, they have included idle machinery, production delays and concerns over pollution norms governing backup generators. For the electricity department, the strike has sharply reduced the workforce available to respond to faults across a network serving around 8.5 lakh consumers in Gurgaon alone.With the unions threatening to decide on an extension beyond October 24 if their demands are not accepted, the prospect of further disruption remains a concern. The government is pursuing a legal challenge to the licence, but until the dispute is resolved and normal operations resume, consumers remain caught between the regulator's decision, the employees' opposition and the state's efforts to restore services.
Article Summary: Three-day strike by Haryana's electricity department employees crippled power supply across Gurgaon on Thursday. Thousands of households went without electricity and water, and nearly 1,800 manufacturing units faced disruption. The disruption exposed the city's dependence on an uninterrupted electricity supply for even its most basic needs.

Article Title: Govt plans colour-coded driving licence for Indians, foreigners
Article Text:
Under the draft, the ministry has listed separate sets of documents for proof of address, age and identity. (Generative image)

Govt plans colour-coded DLs for Indians, foreigners

NEW DELHI: In a first, govt has proposed mentioning the nationality of driving licence holders on DLs and introducing separate colour schemes for Indian andforeign nationals as well as doing away with affidavits sworn before an executive magistrate or notary as proof of age and address, which has the potential of being misused.Life insurance policies, too, would no longer be accepted as proof. Proposing sweeping changes to the driving licence (DL) regime under Motor Vehicles Rules, the road transport ministry Wednesday issued a draft notification to raise the pass mark for the online safe-driving tutorial assessment from the current 60% to 75%.It has also proposed making it mandatory for licences to carry the holder’s blood group, mobile number and emergency contact details. The ministry has proposed waiving fees for specified DL services, including changes to address, name and contact number, if applicants avail themselves of these services through online Aadhaar authentication.At present, if an applicant cannot produce any of the 12 listed documents, the licencing authority “may accept an affidavit sworn before an executive magistrate, judicial magistrate or notary public as proof of age and address”.Anil Chhikara, an expert in motor vehicle licencing, said, “The use of simple affidavits is being phased out after miscreants used them to register false addresses and dates of birth. Applicants must now provide verifiable documents. ”Under the draft, the ministry has listed separate sets of documents for proof of address, age and identity. Address proofs include Aadhaar card, Electoral Photo Identity Card, e-ration card, electricity or gas bills for the preceding three months, and proof of legal presence for foreign nationals. Acceptable age proofs include passports, school board mark sheets, birth certificates and identity cards issued by govt departments. Aadhaar, passports, e-ration cards and PAN have been listed as acceptable identity proofs.The proposed changes aim to curb the submission of false documents, tighten assessment requirements and make licence-related services more accessible. They also seek to streamline online DL services and set timelines for processing applications to change licence particulars.Under the proposal, the safe-driving tutorial would have to last at least 30 minutes, while the higher qualifying score of 75% is intended to make the assessment more stringent. Licencing authorities would have to approve or reject online applications to change DL particulars, including name and address, within 15 days, giving reasons for rejection.An application for a change of address that remains undecided for 30 days would be deemed approved. The draft also proposes a consolidated application form for services such as DL renewal, issuance of duplicate licences, addition of a vehicle class and changes to personal particulars. Specified applicant details would be retrieved electronically from the Sarathi portal wherever available.
Article Summary: Govt plans colour-coded DLs for Indians, foreigners. Life insurance policies, too, would no longer be accepted as proof. Proposed changes aim to curb the submission of false documents. They also seek to streamline online DL services and set timelines for processing applications.

Article Title: CEC impeachment: Speaker Om Birla says fresh motion against Gyanesh Kumar will be examined as per rules
Article Text:
Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday said if the opposition brings any fresh impeachment motion against the country's top poll officer, it will be examined according to rules and procedures.

Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday said any fresh motion seeking the impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar would be examined in accordance with parliamentary rules and procedures, as opposition protests demanding the poll panel chief’s removal intensified over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The opposition has made two attempts to remove Kumar, with notices in the first attempt rejected by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. Notices submitted in the second attempt are still pending in the Upper House.“If any fresh notice comes, we will see and examine it accordingly under rules and procedures,” Birla told a press conference, responding to a question on the possibility of another impeachment motion against the CEC.Protests against Kumar have intensified over the past fortnight, with opposition parties demanding his resignation over alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls. The agitation gathered momentum afterreported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR, alleging that these were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.Under the Constitution, the CEC can be removed only through a parliamentary process similar to that prescribed for the removal of a Supreme Court judge. The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, also provides for the CEC or an Election Commissioner to resign by submitting a written resignation to the President.The removal process is governed by constitutional provisions and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. Once a removal motion is admitted in either House of Parliament, the Speaker or the Rajya Sabha Chairman constitutes a three-member committee to investigate the charges. The panel comprises the Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge, a chief justice of a high court and a distinguished jurist.If the committee finds the charges unsubstantiated, no further action is taken. If it finds the allegations proved, the motion is taken up for consideration in Parliament. Removal requires each House to pass an address supported by a majority of its total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, in the same session.The opposition’s attempts to remove Kumar have brought the Election Commission’s handling of the SIR under renewed scrutiny, with the possibility of another motion now hinging on the formal parliamentary process and the admissibility of any fresh notice.

New Delhi: India slammed a UN special rapporteur’s report which described Pakistan-based gangster Dawood Ibrahim ’s D-company as an India-based criminal group. Pointing to “glaring inaccuracies” in the report, India warned that such incompetence caused tremendous harm to the global body.First secretary in India’s permanent mission to UN, Raghoo Puri, said the outfit and its chief were wanted in India in connection with the 1993 Mumbai blasts . “Let me correct it for the record. Article Title: Hospitals ‘overcharging’ is a malpractice: Govt to Supreme Court
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Govt has admitted before Supreme Court the “malpractice” of hospitals charging patients high MRPs for medicines and consumables, and said it was conscious of the problem, examining it and devising appropriate interventions in consultation with all stakeholders.In an affidavit filed in SC on the issue of capping prices of all medicines and medical consumables, chemicals and fertilisers ministry said that patients have a very low bargaining position with respect to hospitals, resulting in various malpractices. The affidavit noted the irony of India being home to companies making cheap drugs but patients here having to pay way above the manufacturing price, as well as patients being subjected to overcharging by hospitals.“The Indian drug market is fairly competitive, with a large number of pharmaceutical companies in every drug segment, resulting in one of the lowest prices in the world. Ordinarily, where there is substantial competition, there is no need to regulate prices. However, by their very nature, health treatment and pharmaceutical products involve information and bargaining asymmetries between patients on the one hand, and retail pharmacies, hospital pharmacies, hospitals providing treatment and doctors on the other,” the affidavit said.The govt affidavit said a patient has a “very low bargaining position vis-a-vis the hospital, and the patient’s knowledge of drugs, their substitutes and their prices is also very limited”. These bargaining and information asymmetries result in various malpractices in the system despite strong competition among manufacturers, leading to the need for regulation, it said.Enumerating the steps taken by it to control the pricing of drugs, govt said ceiling prices for 935 scheduled formulations and retail prices of 3,881 new drugs have been fixed. Govt filed the affidavit on a plea filed by Dr Sanjay Kulshrestha, who referred to a Niti Aayog report and a 2020 statement of the then health minister Harsh Vardhan that expenditure on health pushed an estimated six crore families below the poverty line each year.The affidavit said hospitals buy medicines from manufacturers who provide highest trade margin and then sell those medicines to patients at MRP, with margins ranging from 170% to 700% or more in the case of anti-cancer drugs.“That another area of concern in the sector is the supply of consumables in hospitals, where margins of 100% to 1000% or more are prevalent, along with a tendency of hospitals to purchase consumables that have a high MRP and margin, with a low price to the distributor/hospital. Ordinarily, hospital supplies are included in the package cost for treatment of major diseases/procedures under govt schemes/insurance, and govt/insurance agencies negotiate and fix the lowest rate for such packages. However, for patients making direct payment to the hospital, hospital supplies are billed separately at MRP,” it said.
Article Summary: Hospitals charge up to 700% premium on cancer drugs. Govt admitted before Supreme Court the ‘malpractice’ of hospitals charging patients high MRPs for medicines and consumables. Indian drug market is fairly competitive, with a large number of pharmaceutical companies in every drug segment, resulting in one of the lowest prices in the world.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday called for stronger global institutions, a greater voice for the Global South and effective international cooperation during crises, while accusing the Congress leadership of repeatedly failing to launch its leader politically.Addressing the NDTV World Summit 2026 in New Delhi, PM Modi said institutions such as the United Nations were struggling to keep pace with the changing world order and emerging challenges, according to news agency ANI.PM Modi warned that trade, technology and sea routes were increasingly being “weaponised”, stressing the need for a global system that prevents the strong from exploiting the vulnerable. NEW DELHI: Looking to further expand their strategic partnership, India and Poland agreed to double bilateral trade by 2030 and announced dialogue mechanisms for defence industrial collaboration and counterterrorism cooperation as PM Narendra Modi hosted his counterpart Donald Tusk for talks Thursday.Modi and Tusk expressed deepest concern in a joint statement over the war in Ukraine, including its tragic humanitarian consequences and the impact on Global South. In his media statement, Modi assured Tusk that whether it is Ukraine or West Asia, India will continue to support every meaningful effort for peace.Poland views the war in Ukraine as a direct threat to its national security and sovereignty due to its shared border, influx of refugees and the threat of future Russian aggression in eastern Europe.“They reiterated the need for a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in line with international law, consistent with the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, including respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity,” said the joint statement. The leaders also noted the negative impacts of the war on global food and energy security, especially for the Global South.Modi and Tusk, the first Polish PM to visit India in 16 years, also backed an MoU under negotiation for cooperation in critical minerals.Modi said the friendship between India and Poland was based not only on diplomatic ties but also on a shared heritage of humanity and empathy. He recalled how, during the Second World War, the royal families of Jamnagar and Kolhapur had provided shelter in India to thousands of Polish children and families. He also thanked Poland for helping India evacuate Indian students from Ukraine shortly after the Russia-Ukraine war began in 2022.Modi said the world was passing through a period of uncertainty and change, and even in such times, both India and Poland were emerging as important hubs of growth, technology and innovation.“Today we have agreed to deepen ties in defence, space and nuclear energy. In all these strategic sectors, we invite Polish companies to engage in co-development and co-production with India,” he said.He also announced a startup bridge to facilitate cooperation in IT, Artificial Intelligence and critical technologies.“Both India and Poland believe in democratic values and the rule of law,” Modi said, underlining that both sides considered reforms essential to make global governance institutions more empowered.The two countries agreed that the UN needed structural reforms, including expansion of UNSC in both permanent and non-permanent categories, to remain relevant, credible and effective. In the joint statement, Poland expressed support for India’s membership of a more inclusive, reformed and expanded UNSC, as well as its candidature for a non-permanent seat on the council for 2028-29.Modi and Tusk unequivocally condemned terrorism, including cross-border terrorism, and stressed that there could be no justification for terrorism on any grounds.“They condemned in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in J&K’s Pahalgam on 22 April, 2025. They called for strong and concerted action against terrorists and terrorist entities, including those designated by the UNSC 1267 sanctions committee,” said the joint statement.Defence and security cooperation was a major focus, with the leaders underlining importance of an Agreement on Mutual Protection and Exchange of Classified Information and expressing expectation it would be signed soon.They proposed a defence industry dialogue to develop a “forward-looking framework for defence industrial cooperation”, including business-to-business engagement and, where mutually agreed, partnerships in technology, co-development, co-production and other forms of collaboration.
Article Summary: Poland views the war in Ukraine as a direct threat to its national security and sovereignty. PM Modi assured Tusk that whether it is Ukraine or West Asia, India will continue to support every meaningful effort for peace. Both sides considered reforms essential to make global governance institutions more empowered.

NEW DELHI: The Cabinet Secretariat did not take any action on complaints filed by two election commissioners against an officer in the Election Commission, saying the letters were written in their “individual capacity” and did not represent the poll panel as a whole, according to documents released in response to an RTI application.Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had separately written to Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan on July 29, raising concerns about the conduct of senior deputy election commissioner Maneesh Garg, an IAS officer appointed to the Commission by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) on September 2, 2024.The letters were provided in an RTI response to activist Commodore Lokesh K Batra (retd).The Indian Express had reported in September that the two Election Commissioners approached the Cabinet Secretary after Garg issued a work allocation order that they believed could concentrate powers over changes to voter records at the central level, instead of allowing officials at the state level to handle them.In a statement on September 26, the Election Commission said the work allocation orders issued by Garg were never implemented following directions from the two Commissioners.The poll panel also said the complaints concerned an officer on deputation and not matters related to policy or the IT division.According to a Cabinet note included in the RTI response, both Commissioners alleged that Garg had issued an order changing the work allocation of officers senior or equivalent to him after taking charge as the link officer of the deputy election commissioner (Administration).The Commissioners said the changes were made without consulting the Commission or the officers concerned. They also alleged that Garg acted despite repeated oral and written instructions against making such changes without prior discussion or approval from the Commission."Both the ECs have stated that Shri Garg, after assuming the charge as link officer of DEC (Admn), has issued an order regarding work allocation of equivalent and senior officers to him without discussing the revised work allocation with the Commission or the officers concerned. Further, the aforementioned ECs have stated that this has happened despite repeated oral and written instructions to all concerned officers against taking such actions without prior discussion/approval of the Commission," the Cabinet note said.The two Commissioners alleged that Garg's actions violated the chief election commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.Joshi also said that when he sought the relevant file from the Administration Division, it was not provided to him.A Cabinet note prepared on August 3 proposed seeking the chief election commissioner's opinion on the complaints."In this connection, we may request the chief election commissioner for his opinion on the issue. Accordingly, a draft DO is put up for approval, please."However, a subsequent note dated August 4 said taking action on complaints from individual Election Commissioners without an official communication from the Commission as a whole could be seen as interference in the functioning of the constitutional body."The Commission is a Constitutional Body and is insulated from executive interference by design to ensure that it functions independently and in a transparent manner. The working and functioning of the Commission are governed by the rules and guidelines of the Election Commission. The above communications are from the Election Commissioners in their individual capacity and, while they must be taken with due seriousness, they cannot be seen as a formal communication from the Commission as a whole," the note said.It added that although Garg had been appointed by the ACC, he was now an officer of the Election Commission, and his work and conduct were governed by the poll panel's rules and guidelines.The note also referred to Section 18 of the 2023 Act, which states that the Commission should conduct its business unanimously as far as possible, with any differences of opinion settled by a majority decision."Election Commissioners have sent these communications for appropriate action; however, in the absence of any official communication from the Commission as a whole, any action at this stage may be inappropriate. It may also be construed as interference in the functioning of the Constitutional Body. Hence, it would be appropriate to send acknowledgement to both Election Commissioners with a copy to PPS to CEC for information of CEC," the note said.The draft note signed by Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan was also marked to the secretary of the department of personnel and training and the establishment officer to keep the matter on record.The note said this would "enable it to be taken into account in future decision-making regarding the officer".Somanathan also signed an acknowledgement letter confirming receipt of the complaints and sent copies to both election commissioners.The letters were acknowledged on August 5, 2026, with copies marked to the department of personnel and training, the Establishment Officer and the office of the chief election commissioner.
Article Summary: Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had separately written to Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan on July 29. They had raised concerns about the conduct of senior deputy election commissioner Maneesh Garg. The Cabinet Secretariat did not take any action on complaints filed by two election commissioners against an officer.

NEW DELHI: Amid SC’s scrutiny of hospitals charging patients steep mark-ups on medicines and consumables, govt officials have flagged gaps in data and regulatory hurdles in extending price controls to hospital supplies, saying the Centre first needs to establish the extent of margins before considering intervention.The Union govt has told the SC in its affidavit that margins on hospital consumables can range from 100% to 1,000% or more, highlighting concerns over the high mark-ups patients often face on supplies used during treatment. However, a senior official told TOI that the govt does not have the data needed to assess margins across hospital supplies and determine whether wider controls are warranted.“We first need to get the data and then examine whether there is a margin and a need to control it,” another senior official said, explaining that the purchase price of medicines and consumables would need to be compared with what hospitals charge patients before deciding on any intervention.Centre fixes ceiling prices for scheduled medicines and has limited annual price increases for non-scheduled drugs up to 10%. It has decided to cap trade margins on certain anti-cancer medicines at 30% of MRP. Extending similar controls to other medicines and hospital consumables, officials said, would require analysis and consultation.A health ministry official, however, raised doubts about how far the govt could regulate hospital billing, saying hospitals, with health being a state subject and governed by the Clinical Establishments Act or other laws enacted by state govts..The Centre’s role, the official said, is largely confined to drug-price regulation through the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority.Regulating individual components of hospital bills would be difficult, the official said, pointing out that hospitals charge package rates without providing detailed itemised bills. Restricting charges on consumables could lead profitconscious hospitals to raise other fees, including surgeons’ charges, the official argued.The official also disputed the blanket use of the term “overcharging” when hospitals bill patients at the MRP, saying there is no general legal requirement to offer discounts below the printed price. They cited delayed reimbursements from insurance firms and govt health schemes as financial pressures on hospitals that would need to be factored in while deciding any broader intervention.
Article Summary: Centre fixes ceiling prices for scheduled medicines and has limited annual price increases for non-scheduled drugs up to 10%. It has decided to cap trade margins on certain anti-cancer medicines at 30% of MRP. Extending similar controls to other medicines and hospital consumables would require analysis and consultation.

Article Title: Natco’s generic SMA drug approved; ‘clinical trial’ labels trigger Kerala row

NEW DELHI: Days after a controversy erupted in Kerala over Natco Pharma’s generic drug for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), regulatory clarifications suggest the row stemmed from labels on bottles supplied free of cost. The words “Physician Sample/Clinical Trial” raised fears among parents that their children were being given medicines meant for clinical trials rather than an authorised drug for routine treatment.In response to queries from TOI, Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) officials said Natco’s risdiplam powder for oral solution (0.75 mg/ml) had been approved by the Telangana State Food and Drug Administration under the applicable regulations. The bulk drug had received CDSCO approval on April 7, 2025.The officials said bioequivalence studies were not required for the oral solution under the regulator’s draft guidance and that additional clinical trials were not necessary before patients could be switched to the generic formulation.Natco said it emerged as the lowest bidder in Kerala’s tender and supplies one free bottle for every three purchased under its Patient Assistance Programme, bringing the effective cost to around ₹8,500 per bottle against ₹1.5 lakh earlier for Roche’s drug.The company acknowledged that the free bottles carry the label “Physician Sample/Clinical trials only”, but said they were supplied as samples under the rate contract and not for clinical trials. It said its generic risdiplam, priced at an MRP of ₹15,900 against ₹6 lakh for Roche’s product, had met regulatory requirements.The issue became a political controversy after Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan said parents of children with SMA had flagged the labels on medicines distributed through SAT Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram. He alleged violations of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules and procurement norms and demanded an inquiry.SAT Hospital authorities have maintained that the medicine distributed was the approved generic formulation, not an experimental drug.Risdiplam is used to treat SMA, a rare genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness. Kerala had been supplying Roche’s branded medicine free to eligible children at a negotiated price. The shift to Natco’s generic version could substantially reduce treatment costs and potentially allow the state to extend support to more patients.The controversy comes amid opposition from parents and the Cure SMA Foundation of India to Kerala’s decision to replace Roche’s medicine with Natco’s generic version. Parents have sought assurances about the safety and efficacy of switching children who have improved on the existing treatment.While the regulatory clarification addresses the generic drug’s approval status, the episode raises a separate question: whether labelling that combines “Physician Sample” and “Clinical Trial” can cause confusion when medicines are supplied for patient use.
Article Summary: Regulatory clarifications suggest the row stemmed from labels on bottles supplied free of cost. The words “Physician Sample/Clinical Trial” raised fears among parents. Natco’s risdiplam powder for oral solution (0.75 mg/ml) had been approved by Telangana State Food and Drug Administration.

Article Title: Dark side of glow-ups: The ugly truth of India's beauty trends and what you need to be aware of
Article Text:
The NMC guidelines do not aim to stop people from seeking treatment. Instead, they aim to ensure that patients make informed medical decisions guided by clinical expertise rather than an algorithm-driven sales pitch.

Dermatology vs cosmetology

The NMC rulebook: What changes on your feed

Shift in strategy: Before vs after the guidelines

Education vs covert marketing

Performance marketing, DMs, and tele-consult safeguards

When aesthetics go wrong: The clinical and human cost

How patients can assess practitioners in the post-hype era

Verify core medical qualifications:

Evaluate the consultation:

Review case examples privately:

Demand clinical assessment and safety protocols:

Putting clinical care ahead of the sales pitch

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Scroll through Instagram on any given Tuesday, and you are bound to hit the "Glow Up" algorithm. With the dramatic "before-and-after" transitions, an influencer gushing over their new "glass skin" chemical peels, and local clinics promising a "100% guaranteed acne cure," cosmetic medicine has officially crossed over into pop culture.It feels less like an invasive clinical procedure and more like buying a new pair of sneakers. One click, instant gratification.In India's hyper-visual, social-media-obsessed culture, looking "filtered" in real life has created a massive boom for cosmetic clinics. But behind the glossy aesthetic lies a wild-west market where non-clinical salon technicians, short-course certificate holders, and non-core medical practitioners are offering everything from laser hair removal to dermal fillers.The reels make the procedures seem cheap and accessible, but the noise creates a great deal of confusion for potential customers and raises risk of botched procedures.To halt this commercial noise and protect patients from predatory marketing, the National Medical Commission (NMC), India's apex regulator for medical practice, has introduced a strict ethical framework.The goal? Drawing a hard line between legitimate clinical care and commercial hype.The biggest source of consumer confusion is the assumption that a "dermatologist" and a "cosmetologist" are the same thing. They aren't.Confusing the two can leave you with severe skin damage.A dermatologist completes a rigorous eight-and-a-half-year medical training pathway, comprising a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) degree followed by a three-year Doctor of Medicine (MD) or Diplomate of National Board (DNB) in Dermatology, Venereology, and Leprosy.It also includes comprehensive hands-on training in clinical pathology, complex skin diseases, dermatosurgery, and laser medicine. Similarly, a plastic surgeon undergoes specialized post-doctoral surgical training (MCh or DNB) in reconstructive and aesthetic surgery.On the flip side, "cosmetology" is not a recognized medical specialty or postgraduate qualification under the National Medical Commission (NMC) framework.In practice, the term often describes salon estheticians, technicians, or non-core operators who hold short 3- to 6-month diploma certificates from private, unaccredited institutes.Under the regulatory mandates of the NMC's ethics, non-core practitioners, non-clinical operators, and salon technicians are strictly prohibited from procedures such as laser resurfacing, deep chemical peels, hair transplants, or injectable dermal fillers.As Dr Tanvi Gupta Arora, dermatology consultant at CK Birla Hospital says, "Earlier, there was no term like 'cosmetology' in medical residency. Aesthetic procedures were an integrated part of our clinical curriculum under Dermatosurgery, complete with hands-on surgical training under senior guides.”She adds, “The challenge in India is that regulations were historically lax. Non-clinical entities like salon technicians and short-course diploma holders started performing deep chemical peels, aggressive lasers, and recommending fillers without clinical supervision."If your favorite clinic's social media page suddenly looks a lot quieter, blame (or thank) the NMC rules.Now, doctors cannot post promotional "before-and-after" grid shots, transition reels, or retouched result photos on public feeds. Clinical photos are strictly restricted to anonymized, scientific, or educational use. They set clear boundaries on how practitioners can advertise their services, use social media and engage with influencers.Influencer barter crackdown: Free Botox, fillers, or hair transplants given to social media influencers in exchange for "spontaneous" glowing reviews are now outright banned. Doctors cannot solicit or feature patient video testimonials or star-rating screenshots.Killing Superlatives & Guarantees: Phrases like "Best Dermatologist in Delhi," "No. 1 Plastic Surgeon," or "100% Glass Skin Guarantee" are illegal. Doctors are also prohibited from claiming non-existent qualifications (like US-style "Board Certified Plastic Surgeon" titles, which do not exist in India).AI & Pay-Per-Lead Bans: AI-generated "synthetic" patient cases, face filters, or synthetic doctor voices are prohibited without explicit disclaimers. Furthermore, clinics cannot pay marketing agencies "per-patient" commissions.As Dr Vivek Gupta, plastic & cosmetic surgery consultant at Madhukar Rainbow Children’s Hospital, Delhi views it, “In a field where social media creates unrealistic expectations, decisions must be guided by clinical suitability rather than promotional claims. Restrictions on promotional photographs and testimonials mean we must adapt our communication strategies.”He also says how he has upgraded the advertising guidelines for his own clinic. “Our clinic now focuses on expert-led public health education rather than promoting individual outcomes," he says.The daily operational shift across Indian aesthetic clinics is stark.In the earlier, largely unregulated aesthetic medicine market described in the draft, clinics relied on visuals that showcased dramatic transformations and could create the impression that similar results were achievable for everyone.Under the NMC-compliant approach, clinics shift towards educational content, such as anatomical diagrams, procedure explainers and skin-science reels.Rather than promoting individual treatment outcomes, these formats help explain medical conditions, how procedures work and what patients should understand before considering treatment.Dr. Vivek Gupta acknowledges that while digital platforms remain an important source of information for people exploring aesthetic options, restricting promotional material presents a distinct communication challenge."Restrictions on testimonials, promotional photographs, and advertising can make it harder to communicate treatment outcomes and recovery experiences," he says.However, he maintains that "the solution lies in adapting communication strategies rather than compromising ethical standards. Clearer guidance on distinguishing medical education from commercial promotion would help practitioners remain informative while complying with professional regulations."He explains that his practice uses digital platforms to discuss common cosmetic concerns, treatment options, recovery expectations, and potential risks, such as acne scars or skin aging, while strictly avoiding exaggerated claims or guaranteed results."The objective is to build credibility through scientifically accurate information and responsible communication rather than promotional testimonials," he explains.This strategic overhaul also extends to how doctors manage public interaction on digital platforms. Dr. Tanvi Gupta Arora notes that sponsored endorsements and flashing contact numbers over educational reels are now firmly off-limits."Under the guidelines, we cannot do sponsored product endorsements or flash clinic phone numbers over educational videos," she points out, "If I post an educational reel about acne, I turn off comments to prevent direct social media prescribing. We redirect inquiries through proper clinical consultations or telemedicine."In her experience, this levels the playing field for doctors who built their practice on "clinical labor rather than massive ad budgets."In an era where skincare trends go viral overnight on reels and shorts, the distinction between public health awareness and disguised product placement has grown dangerously blurry.The NMC’s crackdown directly addresses this hidden marketplace by prohibiting barter deals where influencers trade shoutouts for free treatments.Dr Vivek Gupta highlights that the true test of educational content lies in its intent and presentation."The distinction lies in the information's purpose and presentation. Public health education helps people understand cosmetic concerns, treatment options, preventive measures, and potential risks," he explains, "Covert marketing uses educational content to promote a particular procedure or commercial interest. Every communication should prioritise scientific accuracy, balanced information, and patient welfare rather than encouraging people to purchase a specific service or product. "When asked about using non-medical influencers, Dr Gupta reveals he has never relied on them for endorsements."Aesthetic treatments require individual assessment, and their suitability, risks, and outcomes vary from person to person. Influencers can help raise awareness about skincare, but personal experiences should never be mistaken for medical evidence," he says, adding that credibility in this field "should ultimately come from clinical expertise and responsible patient care."Instead of chasing influencer viral loops, his clinic prioritizes expert-led educational content, media interactions, and public awareness initiatives.He asserts, "Trust is also established during consultations, where patients receive realistic expectations, understand potential risks and learn about alternatives. This approach places greater emphasis on clinical credibility than online popularity. In aesthetic care, sustainable trust comes from transparent communication, professional competence and a consistent commitment to patient welfare."The regulatory overhaul doesn't just stop at Instagram reels; it reshapes the entire digital sales funnel used by modern cosmetic chains.Historically, aesthetic marketing relied heavily on aggressive performance marketing campaigns. Clickbait advertisements proclaiming "Get glass skin in 3 days" or "call now for 50% off hair transplants" were explicitly designed to exploit appearance-related insecurities, feeding directly into pay-per-lead models.Under the new guidelines, performance marketing must be stripped of high-pressure sales tactics, artificial urgency, and guaranteed outcome claims.Dr Vivek Gupta emphasizes that digital visibility must remain factual and consistent with medical ethics requirements."Campaigns should avoid guaranteed outcomes, misleading claims, patient testimonials used for promotion, and messaging that exploits appearance-related insecurities," he states, adding that marketing agencies must understand these boundaries.This shift has also forced a total overhaul of digital triage and initial online consultations. In the past, prospective patients could drop a comment under a video or send a direct message (DM) detailing their skin issues, receiving direct prescriptions or treatment quotes from social media managers.Dr Gupta stresses the vital difference between general inquiries and actual consultations, noting, "Digital messages can provide basic information, but individual treatment recommendations require an appropriate clinical assessment."For tele-consultations, safeguards such as identity verification, informed consent, confidentiality, and proper documentation are essential."Photographs shared online may not provide sufficient information to determine treatment suitability. Where physical examination or a detailed assessment is necessary, patients should be advised to attend an in-person consultation," he warns, concluding that "convenience must never override clinical judgement, privacy or patient safety."When cosmetic procedures are marketed like fast-fashion beauty products, patients pay a heavy price with their physical and financial well-being.Both dermatologists and plastic surgeons frequently find themselves functioning as corrective specialists, tasked with repairing severe damage caused by non-core practitioners or aggressive "assembly-line" cosmetic chains.For instance, in a September 30 order, the Bengaluru urban district consumer disputes redressal commission held a clinic liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice after a woman suffered second-degree facial burns during laser hair removal in April.The commission directed the clinic to refund the Rs 1,100 procedure fee with interest, pay Rs 1 lakh in damages and Rs 10,000 in litigation costs, giving it 45 days to comply.Dr Tanvi Gupta Arora highlights how these botched cases unfold in daily practice, pointing out that aggressive commercial chains routinely lure vulnerable patients into spending massive sums on guaranteed outcomes."Some of these cosmetology chains, what they are doing is they are running these advertisements that 'we will just cure your pigmentation, you will be 100% free of your pigmentation.' And people, they fall into the trap and go and spend thousands or lakhs with no result," Dr Tanvi explains.When these uncalibrated procedures fail, patients are thrown back into the market with damaged skin and exhausted finances.Dr Tanvi notes that treating these complications requires extensive time and care before even touching the patient's original cosmetic concern."Sometimes the damages are irreversible. You had so much damage that you now cannot treat it," she shares, adding: "So you have to further do more procedures. Like sometimes these patients come to me with even worse pigmentation. First I have to spend two to three months correcting that issue, the skin has become thin or it has become burnt, and then we talk about the pigmentation correction."The experts map out certain points that a patient could look for to assess the authenticity of the clinic or expert.Patients should look for recognised postgraduate qualifications, such as an MD or DNB in dermatology or an MCh or DNB in Plastic Surgery, and verify registration details with the state medical council or NMC register.Dr Vivek Gupta stresses the importance of qualifications and competence: "Plastic surgeons and dermatologists have different areas of expertise, and the procedures offered must align with their respective training and applicable scope of practice. Non-core practitioners must not misrepresent their qualifications or undertake procedures beyond their competence. Patients should be able to verify credentials and understand who is performing a procedure. "Consultations should offer factual information about diagnosis, risks, alternatives and realistic outcomes, without guarantees or pressure to proceed.Dr Vivek Gupta explains: "Trust is established during consultations, where patients receive realistic expectations, understand potential risks and learn about alternatives. This approach places greater emphasis on clinical credibility than online popularity.”He also cautions against relying on online reviews to judge clinical capability: "Instead of promotional testimonials, patients should focus on recognised qualifications, relevant experience, consultation quality, and transparent discussions about risks, alternatives, and recovery."Instead of public promotional posts, patients can ask to see clinical case records during a consultation to understand the likely scope and outcomes of a procedure.Dr Tanvi Gupta Arora says: "Before and after photos should not be on your social media. You can put it on your website, or if somebody comes to your clinic, then any day they can come to your clinic and then you can show them the before and after pictures or whatever particular procedure they are looking for."Patients should ensure that clinics conduct appropriate assessments, use approved devices and injectables, and have emergency procedures to manage adverse reactions. Digital messages and photographs may not be sufficient to determine whether a procedure is suitable.Dr Vivek Gupta emphasises: "Digital messages can provide basic information, but individual treatment recommendations require an appropriate clinical assessment... Photographs shared online may not provide sufficient information to determine treatment suitability. Where physical examination or a detailed assessment is necessary, patients should be advised to attend an in-person consultation. Convenience must never override clinical judgement, privacy or patient safety. "The NMC guidelines aim to curb predatory marketing, banning influencer barter culture, and restricting invasive procedures strictly to qualified specialists.For clinics and marketing agencies, this transition demands a total overhaul of digital strategy, swapping sensationalism, clickbait, and artificial transformation grids for transparent, expert-led public education.For patients, the rules offer much-needed protection in a market that has grown dangerously confusing. A cosmetic procedure is not an off-the-rack beauty buy; it is a medical intervention carried out on living human tissue. Ultimately, the new regulatory landscape encourages consumers to value what truly matters when choosing a doctor: prioritizing clinical expertise, authentic qualifications, and patient safety over an algorithm-driven sales pitch.
Article Summary: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has introduced a strict ethical framework. The goal is to draw a hard line between legitimate clinical care and commercial hype. The biggest source of consumer confusion is the assumption that "dermatologist" and "cosmetologist" are the same thing.

Article Title: Defence, space & nuclear energy: PM Modi, Poland's Tusk bat for deeper ties, doubling trade by 2030

India, Poland to deepen

strategic cooperation

India, Poland aim to double bilateral trade by 2030

PM Modi recalls shared history of India-Poland ties

Jaishankar calls on Polish Prime Minister

Tusk on three-day visit to India
